papers.title: The Impact of Social Insurance on Household Debt
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how the expansion of social insurance affects households’ accumulation of debt. Insurance can reduce reliance on debt by lessening the financial impact of adverse events such as illness and job loss. But it can also weaken the motive to self-insure through savings, and households’ improved financial resilience can increase access to credit. Using data on 10 million people and a quasi-experimental research design, we estimate the causal effect of expanded insurance on household debt, exploiting ZIP-level heterogeneity in exposure to the staggered expansions of one of the largest US social insurance programs: Medicaid. We find that a 1 percentage point increase in a ZIP code’s Medicaid-eligible population increases credit card borrowing by 0.38%. Decomposing this effect in a model of household borrowing, we show that increased credit supply in response to households’ improved financial resilience drives the rise in borrowing and contributes 30% of the net welfare gains of expanding Medicaid.

papers.title: The Impact of the Great Recession on Mortality: A Dynamic Factor Analysis
papers.abstract: We use a dynamic factor time series model to estimate the national mortality impact of the Great Recession. In aggregate, the Great Recession reduced the average annual, age-adjusted mortality rate by about 2 percent, with effects persisting for at least a decade. In a calibrated model of the welfare effects of the estimated impacts of the Great Recession on consumption and mortality, we find that the welfare gain from the estimated mortality decline is quantitatively significant relative to the welfare loss from the estimated consumption decline. The estimated mortality decline is also quantitatively close to prior mortality estimates using cross-sectional variation in the severity of the Great Recession, implying limited general equilibrium effects of the Great Recession on mortality. More broadly, our findings suggest that prior evidence from local labor markets that recessions are good for health can be extrapolated to the likely mortality consequences of nationwide recessions.

papers.title: Transportation as a Barrier to Education Access: Evidence from Chicago Public Schools
papers.abstract: School choice can weaken the link between residential neighborhood and educational opportunity only if students can reach the schools available to them. We study school choice in Chicago, where high schoolers can choose among schools throughout the city but generally rely on public transit, making the structure of the transit network a key determinant of opportunity. Using student-level rankings and public transit travel times, we document two systematic patterns: Black students are less likely to rank top-rated schools first and face longer public transit times to such schools. We estimate a discrete choice model to separate the value placed on schools from the costs of reaching them. We find that high schools vary substantially in how they are valued and that there is a high degree of agreement across racial groups in their relative ranking. However, transit times vary significantly across neighborhoods, generating racial differences in demand for top-rated schools. Counterfactually, giving Black students the travel times of white students increases demand for top-rated schools by 23 percentage points. Finally, we identify underserved neighborhoods where public transit access constrains demand and quantify how targeted bus service would increase demand for high-quality schools. Our counterfactuals quantify how transportation expands school access.

papers.title: Will Medical Care Strangle or Save the Federal Budget?
papers.abstract: Forecasts of the federal budget depend greatly on trends in medical spending. Since 1970, medical spending has nearly tripled as a share of gross domestic product (GDP). However, spending growth has barely exceeded GDP growth since 2010. This difference in growth rates makes forecasting spending difficult. I present scenarios for future spending derived from considering the sources of spending increase, ranging from rapid increases in new, expensive treatments to a reduction in spending due to cost-reducing technology. Even modest increases in spending relative to GDP are likely to overwhelm the federal government’s ability to pay for medical care using current tax instruments.

papers.title: Staying Connected: Experimental Effects of Coach-Delivered Text Messages in an Adult High School
papers.abstract: More than 23 million adults in the United States lack a high school diploma, and most who return to school drop out before graduating. We evaluate a randomized intervention of adult high school students in which coaches delivered text messages that encouraged persistence. We find that assignment to treatment increased graduation by 4.9 percentage points, and the effect of message receipt among compliers is 9.3 percentage points, a 41 percent increase relative to the control mean. The intervention operated on the intensive margin by increasing the number of courses completed, but did not affect student enrollment. The effects of the intervention are concentrated among students assigned to experienced coaches, who customized their messages more extensively. We contextualize the economic impact of the low-cost intervention by comparing labor market earnings of graduates to non-graduates, which implies an earnings benefit of $149 per treated student over four years.

papers.title: Correcting for Heterogeneity in the Use of Subjective Scales
papers.abstract: Analyses of survey data may be confounded if people use response scales differently. We formalize and generalize the theory behind using “calibration questions,” such as vignettes, to correct for scale-use heterogeneity. Finding, in our (N ≈ 10,000) and existing data, that the mapping between respondents’ scales is approximately linear, we develop a simple estimator for scale-use-corrected regressions. We validate it using subjective-scale ratings of height and weight and illustrate it with life satisfaction regressions, where correction leaves the main qualitative findings intact but can substantially change coefficient ratios, for example tripling the estimated cost of unemployment relative to income.
